standard.title: Consumer and Financial Risk
standard.description: how individuals and businesses manage consumer and financial risks and rewards
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y8 (direct predecessor AC9HE8K05): processes individuals and businesses use to plan and budget to achieve short- and long-term financial objectives. From Y7 (AC9HE7K05): consumer rights and responsibilities of individuals and businesses relating to financial products and services. Students understand planning, budgeting and consumer rights but have not yet studied active risk management strategies — the move from understanding what rights exist to understanding how to manage active threats.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how individuals and businesses manage consumer and financial risks and rewards.

nodes.label: Types of consumer and financial risk
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and discuss examples of consumer and financial risk to individuals and businesses, including scams, identity theft and fraudulent transactions.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe two types of consumer or financial risk (e.g. scams, identity theft) and explain how each affects individuals or businesses.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss the range of consumer and financial risks to individuals and businesses from the elaboration examples: scams (phishing, investment scams, social engineering), identity theft (unauthorised use of personal information for financial gain), and fraudulent transactions (unauthorised payments, card fraud). Explain how each type affects individuals and businesses differently in terms of financial loss, reputational damage and emotional harm.
wider: Investigate current scam types targeting Australian consumers and businesses (using ACCC Scamwatch data) and analyse which demographic groups are most affected and why
Examine how cybersecurity incidents in businesses create consumer financial risk — using a real Australian data breach case to trace consequences for both the business and affected customers
Analyse how social media and digital platforms have created new categories of consumer and financial risk that did not exist a decade ago
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish between risk types will be unable to match appropriate management strategies to specific risks in subsequent nodes — applying insurance to a scam, for example, is not meaningful risk management and reflects category confusion.

response_modes.reason: Risk categories (scams, identity theft, fraud) each have distinct mechanisms. Building a repertoire of current, realistic examples from Australian contexts — not abstract definitions — makes the subsequent strategy-matching work genuine.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct types of consumer or financial risk
Describes how each risk type affects individuals or businesses
Distinguishes between risk types rather than treating them as equivalent

nodes.label: Consumer reward programs and financial rewards
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss examples of consumer reward programs and financial rewards, including loyalty schemes and investment returns.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one consumer reward program and one type of financial reward (e.g. investment return) and explain how each benefits individuals or businesses.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss examples of consumer rewards from the elaboration range: innovative products and services that reward early adopters; benefits accrued through loyalty schemes (frequent flyer points, cashback, member discounts); and rewards for building savings and making investments (interest on term deposits, dividends from shares, capital growth from home ownership). Explain how each rewards mechanism functions and who benefits.
wider: Investigate the economics of loyalty programs — examining how businesses profit from them while appearing to reward consumers — and evaluate whether loyalty programs are genuinely beneficial for consumers or primarily for businesses
Examine how the rewards from home ownership vary across income levels and geographic locations in Australia, and discuss what this reveals about equity in financial reward distribution
Compare investment rewards available to young Australians (micro-investing, superannuation, first home saver accounts) and analyse which reward mechanisms are most accessible

response_modes.reason: Reward mechanisms differ significantly across loyalty programs, savings products and investment assets. Multiple examples prevent students from conflating reward types and support a balanced risk-reward discussion in the final node.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The equity dimension of financial rewards — who has access to investment returns, whether loyalty programs genuinely benefit consumers — offers rich analytical contexts that connect economic concepts to social fairness arguments.
success_criteria: Describes at least two types of consumer or financial reward with examples
Explains how each reward mechanism functions
Uses terms such as 'loyalty scheme', 'investment returns', 'savings'

nodes.label: Individual strategies to manage consumer and financial risk
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain strategies individuals use to manage consumer and financial risk, including goal-setting, insurance, savings and scam alertness.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain two strategies individuals use to manage consumer or financial risk (e.g. maintaining a savings buffer, checking for scams before engaging).
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain the range of strategies individuals use to manage consumer and financial risk from the elaboration examples: setting financial goals (having a plan reduces impulsive decisions and builds resilience); maintaining insurance (transfers risk of major losses); building savings (provides a buffer against unexpected financial shocks); and being alert to scams (recognising warning signs, verifying contacts, using official channels). Explain how each strategy reduces exposure to specific risks.
wider: Investigate how financial literacy levels in Australia vary by demographic group and analyse how this affects individuals' capacity to implement risk management strategies
Examine the role of government consumer protection resources (e.g. ASIC's MoneySmart, ACCC Scamwatch) in supporting individual risk management — evaluating whether they are effective

Analyse a case where an individual failed to use available risk management strategies and experienced significant consumer or financial harm — identifying which strategies, if applied, would have reduced the risk

response_modes.reason: Strategy-to-risk matching requires systematic reasoning: risk type → strategy that addresses it → mechanism by which the strategy reduces exposure. Without this structure, students list strategies without connecting them to specific risks.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two strategies individuals use to manage consumer or financial risk
Explains the mechanism by which each strategy reduces exposure to risk
Matches strategies to appropriate risk types

nodes.label: Business practices for consumer protection and ethical decision-making
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify business practices that protect consumer safety and reflect on the importance of ethical decision-making and corporate social responsibility in consumer and financial contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one practice businesses use to protect consumer safety (e.g. mandatory product standards, cooling-off periods) and explain why ethical decision-making matters for consumers and businesses.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain practices businesses use to protect consumer safety: mandatory and voluntary standards (product safety requirements), product safety recalls (removing dangerous products from market), and cooling-off periods (allowing consumers to reverse financial decisions). Reflect on the importance of ethical decision-making and corporate social responsibility when making consumer and financial decisions — including consequences for customers, families, communities and the environment.
wider: Investigate a specific Australian product recall or consumer protection enforcement action and analyse what the business did, what it should have done, and the consequences of its actions for consumers and its own reputation

Examine how corporate social responsibility reporting has changed expectations of business ethical behaviour in Australia, and whether voluntary CSR commitments effectively protect consumers or whether mandatory standards are needed

Analyse how Indigenous consumer protection issues (e.g. predatory financial products targeting remote communities) reveal gaps in Australia's consumer protection system and what businesses and government should do differently

response_modes.reason: This node integrates risk types (Node 1), rewards (Node 2), and individual strategies (Node 3) into an account of how businesses manage the risk-reward relationship on behalf of consumers. Students should connect: what risks exist → what rewards are offered → how businesses protect consumers from harm while offering rewards.

Ethical decision-making requires students to reason about consequences across multiple stakeholders simultaneously. A stakeholder consequence framework (individual consumer → family → community → environment) structures the reflection so students move beyond 'ethics is good' generalisations.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two business practices that protect consumer safety
Explains why ethical decision-making and CSR are important in consumer and financial contexts
Considers consequences for multiple stakeholders (individuals, community, environment)
